To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HPV activate the DDR to allow for successful viral replication, that TopBP1 is a key DDR protein in HPV replication, that Top2 is a key protein in the replication of the viral and cellular genome, that the HPV E2 protein is essential for the resolution of DNA structures created during replication, and that the HPV E1 protein is required to maintain the replication fork in the presence of Top2 and TopBP1.
HPV activate the DDR to resolve aberrant DNA structures on viral DNA and that the resolution of these structures is necessary for viral replication to proceed.
HPV replication requires the activation of the DDR to resolve DNA damage that occurs on the viral genome during infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how viral and cellular DNA replication proceeds in the presence of DNA damage signals, and how the virus and the cell can co-exist and persist with an activated DDR.
understanding how HPV activate the DDR, how viral and cellular DNA replication proceeds in the presence of activated DDR proteins, and how the DDR is inactivated in HPV infected cells.
the role of the DNA damage checkpoint and its regulation by HPV16 in order to understand how the virus can successfully complete replication in the presence and activation of the DDR.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV activation of the DDR is a requirement for viral replication, and that HPV16 infected cells maintain a DDR in an active but attenuated state to allow cellular replication to proceed.
HPV16 activation of the DDR is essential for a successful viral replication cycle and that HPV16 and host replication can proceed in the presence an active DDR.
HPV activation of the DDR is a necessary consequence of HPV replication, and HPV replication in the absence of an active DDR would be unsuccessful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TopBP1 is a key DDR protein that is required for HPV16 replication and that HPV16 E1 and E2 proteins are required to activate the DDR in order to promote HPV16 replication.
the HPV16 E1 replication protein is a key player in the DDR, but that it also functions to resolve aberrant DNA structures on viral DNA in the presence of the DDR.

HPV16 replication in the presence or absence of DDR proteins is an essential step in the HPV16 life cycle and the resolution of these DNA structures on HPV genomes is required for the successful replication of the virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HPV activation of the DDR is essential for viral replication and the DDR is not an anti-viral mechanism.
HPV16 replication is a highly regulated process, and that the activation of the DDR is an important part of this regulation.
DDR proteins and pathways are essential for the HPV life cycle, and thus, targeting DDR pathways could be a novel therapeutic strategy for treating HPV cancers.
